bill_description: S.J.Res.88 is a joint resolution, a type of bill that becomes law if it is enacted. This text is the version the Senate approved on October 30, 2025. It would end the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. A tax on imports is also called a tariff. Ending the emergency would cancel the tariffs based on it: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries. It would not end tariffs under other laws. Each reason compares two situations on October 30, 2025: the law in force that day, and the same law with this bill in effect.

claims.title: The bill ends the April 2 emergency
claims.statement: If enacted, S.J.Res.88 ends the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, in Executive Order 14257, on the date of enactment.
claims.classification_reason: Direct bill text, checked word for word against the packet's bill text. No packet source disputes what the text says.
claims.source_quote: the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution
claims.scope_html: This is the version the Senate approved on October 30, 2025. The comparison is this bill taking effect on that date versus the law in force on that date. The bill names this one emergency only.
claims.background_html: A national emergency is a formal statement by the President that unlocks special legal powers. An executive order is a written order from the President. A joint resolution is a type of bill that becomes law if it is enacted.
claims.support_html: The bill says “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [SES 1]

claims.title: The taxes based on the emergency stop for new imports
claims.statement: When this emergency ends, the extra import taxes imposed because of it stop for new imports at the rates in force that day. Other tariff laws are not ended, and matters already pending or duties already owed are not changed by the ending itself.
claims.classification_reason: Follows directly from the termination law's text applied to taxes the order imposes under this emergency. The packet has no objection; an analysis of ending the same emergency reaches the same result.
claims.source_quote: any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date
claims.scope_html: This covers imports still taxed under this emergency on October 30, 2025. Customs applies these taxes to goods “other than those that fall within the identified exceptions” [SES 3]. For China, covered goods “will be assessed an additional ad valorem duty rate of 10%.” [TR 3] Goods added to the metal tariff lists in August are affected only for their other content: “The non-steel and non-aluminum content will remain subject to the reciprocal and other applicable tariffs.” [UNN 4] The law also says the ending “shall not affect” pending matters or “any rights or duties that matured or penalties that were incurred prior to such date” [SES 2].
claims.background_html: A tariff is a tax on goods brought into a country. The taxes under this emergency are called “reciprocal tariffs”. Later orders changed the rates, but the emergency stayed their basis: “the terms of Executive Order 14257, as amended, shall continue to apply.” [UNN 2]
claims.support_html: Federal law says that when an emergency ends, “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [SES 2]. The Center for American Progress, a policy group that favors ending these taxes, says that ending this emergency “would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [UNN 3]

claims.title: Tariff pressure behind the promises in the deals
claims.statement: Ending these taxes would remove an incentive and an enforcement tool for getting Malaysia and Cambodia to carry out the promises in their signed deals, including promises on market access, labor rights, the environment, security and supply, public rule-making and internet rules.
claims.classification_reason: Adequately sourced, and no retained response challenges this step. The April 2 order itself lists weak labor and environmental standards among the practices it addresses and allows lower rates if a partner remedies such practices. The September order ties relief to partners' commitments, and the deals contain these promises and allow action for not following 'a provision'. The Trade Representative says tariffs can go back into place. The remaining limits (not yet in force, no tariff action yet, general clause, other tools) do not deny that the tool existed on the comparison date. The response to SES_oppose_04 targets a later link and stays local.
claims.scope_html: The deals were signed but not in force on October 30, 2025. This statement concerns whether the tool existed on that date, not whether it had been used or how much it would achieve. The Trade Representative's own examples are “actually opening their market, [and] making the investment and purchase commitments they've agreed to.” [UNT 13] The enforcement article allows action “in accordance with applicable domestic law” [UNN 35] and does not name tariffs. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules set no product-level environmental conditions. Some promises are limited by their wording: Malaysia cooperates “in a manner consistent with applicable requirements of domestic laws and regulations” [SES 40], and its cyber clause says “may include” [SES 40]. The sources reviewed for this statement show no tariff action tied to one of these promises. Other U.S. trade laws also allow responses in some cases.
claims.background_html: Tariff relief means lowering these taxes on a country's goods. An incentive here means a reason for another government to act, because it wants lower U.S. taxes. An enforcement tool means a way to respond if a government breaks a promise. The U.S. Trade Representative is the U.S. official who leads trade talks.
claims.support_html:
The April 2 order lists among the practices it addresses “failures by governments in protecting labor and environment standards” [UNC 10] and “weak labor, environmental, and other regulatory standards and protections” [UNC 10]. It allows lower rates if a partner takes “significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters” [UNC 10]. The September order says earlier rate suspensions were “to reflect the fact that some trading partners had signaled a willingness to undertake meaningful economic and national security commitments with the United States” [SES 32].

The Malaysia statement lists promises in the same deal as the tariff terms: “Malaysia has committed to adopt and maintain high levels of environmental protection and to effectively enforce its environmental laws” [UNC 26] and “Malaysia has committed to refrain from banning, or imposing quotas on, exports to the United States of critical minerals or rare earth elements.” [UNC 26] The enforcement article applies if a country “has not complied with a provision of this Agreement” [UNN 35]. The Trade Representative said that if partners do not honor their agreements, “the president has his tariff authority,” [UNT 13] and that countries that do not comply “can have the tariffs go back into place.” [UNT 13] CNBC said it is not difficult to imagine that a country that agreed to buy goods “in order to avoid higher U.S. tariff rates might go back on that pledge” [UNT 13] if the court ruled against the tariffs.

Point 1 It lowers a cost barrier to replacing fossil fuels with less polluting power.

  • Because By September 2025, the basic import tax under this emergency had raised solar costs: “the baseline tariffs remained in effect and contributed to price increases across solar market segments” [5].
  • Because In April, before the higher rate on China was suspended, an energy consultant named imported storage and power equipment among the goods most affected: “Grid-scale batteries and solar panels, as well as power transformers, are among the hardest hit by price increases on imports” [6].
  • Because The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, warned in April that the taxes would also raise the cost of building clean energy factories, because they apply to imported inputs such as “cement, construction equipment” [7].
  • So Ending these extra taxes reduces a cost barrier to installing clean power and to building the factories that supply it.
  • Because Storage helps clean power replace fossil fuels: “Batteries allow renewables to replace fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal, while keeping a steady flow of power when sources like wind and solar are not producing.” [6]
  • Because Fossil fuel pollution harms plants and animals: “SO 2 causes acid rain, which is harmful to plants and to animals that live in water.” [8]
  • Because Burning fossil fuels also heats the planet: “Burning oil and gas emits greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, which trap heat in the atmosphere and warm the planet” [9].
  • Because Warming damages natural areas on land, in water and around ice. The U.N. climate science panel finds: “Climate change has caused substantial damages, and increasingly irreversible losses, in terrestrial, freshwater, cryospheric, and coastal and open ocean ecosystems (high confidence).” [10]
  • So Making that replacement easier supports [NAME]'s goal of protecting nature from air pollution and warming.

  • Because China's charge has moved with U.S.-China talks. After negotiations in Geneva, it “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” [25] charge.
  • Because The emergency also allows further U.S. tariff increases in response to retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order” [26]. Point 2 Easing costs gives small business owners a fairer chance to keep their livelihoods and the jobs they support.

  • Because The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a business group, reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs” [8].
  • Because Small firms have fewer ways to handle tariff costs than larger rivals. CNBC explains: “Their margins are slimmer, their supply chains less diverse and their negotiating power with vendors dampened by the smaller sizes of their orders.” [9]
  • Because These costs can take money away from jobs. At Reekon Tools, “The hundreds of thousands of dollars Reed planned to use to hire between three and five designers and engineers is now going to tariffs instead, he said.” [9]
  • So Ending the emergency's taxes frees money that affected firms need to operate and hire. It removes a burden that people running smaller firms are less able to absorb. That supports fair opportunities to earn a living for owners and workers.

arguments.title: Ending this source of sudden tax changes protects access to jobs and safe work.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Ending this source of sudden tax changes protects access to jobs and safe work.

  • Because The order allows further tax rises, including power to “increase duties under this order” [10].
  • Because Uncertainty about tariff rates holds back staffing. In its June 2025 survey of firms in the Fourth Federal Reserve District (a region served by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland), the Cleveland Fed found that “19 percent of contacts said that tariff-related uncertainty had led their firm to scale back staffing plans” [11].
  • Because Uncertainty also threatens workers' protection abroad. Asked about tariff uncertainty, Sara Park of the International Labour Organization (ILO) explained: “During periods of crisis or uncertainty, investment generally pauses. One concern is that factories stop investing in improving working conditions, which could affect occupational safety and health.” [12]
  • So Ending the emergency removes its power to change these tax rates again. That removes a source of pressure to hold back hiring and safety improvements. Protecting opportunities to find paid work and stay safe at work serves [NAME]'s concern for workers, including vulnerable workers abroad.
arguments.con_html:
Response Closing one route for sudden tax changes does not establish less uncertainty about the rates firms would actually pay. This response does not deny that the bill ends this order's own power to raise rates.

  • Because Replacement plans were announced before the vote. In a May interview transcribed in a June 2 court filing, trade adviser Peter Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [13] This was a stated plan to keep the tariff policy after losing its emergency-law basis.
  • Because An October analysis described a possible bridge to other tariff powers: “Five months of Section 122 tariffs would provide time for the Commerce Department to do the investigation required by Section 232 of the Trade Act of 1962 for a president to impose tariffs for national security reasons.” [14] Section 122’s use would still have to meet that law’s conditions.
  • So Hiring and safety plans respond to uncertainty about future rates, whichever law sets them. Given the announced search for replacement powers, the PRO's evidence does not establish that ending this legal route would make rates more predictable.

arguments.title: Removing a proven trigger for retaliation reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Removing a proven trigger for retaliation reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.

  • Because China directly answered the April taxes with taxes on U.S. exports. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, says that “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [15].
  • Because Retaliation puts sellers at a disadvantage: “Foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports make U.S. goods less competitive in foreign markets compared to goods not subject to tariffs” [15]. October reporting shows what this can mean for farm income: one Minnesota grower was selling soybeans “for less than what it cost to produce them.” [16]
  • Because Reducing the U.S. taxes has already helped ease this conflict. The May joint agreement paired U.S. tariff cuts with China's commitment to “suspend or remove the non-tariff countermeasures taken against the United States since April 2, 2025.” [17]
  • So Ending this tariff trigger and its power to fuel new rounds of retaliation reduces an avoidable risk to export sales. Protecting people whose livelihoods are caught in that conflict gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: China's March farm duties responded to a U.S. action separate from the April emergency. On October 30, 2025, China said the U.S. would suspend the 24 percent reciprocal tariff for another year and that China would adjust its countermeasures, and reported consensus on expanding agricultural trade. The May deal left China's 10 percent charge in place. Sources: [15], [18], [17].

Evidence note: On February 26, 2026, after U.S. Customs stopped collecting IEEPA tariffs and began a Section 122 surcharge, China's commerce ministry said it would assess those measures and then decide whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs. It also noted U.S. statements about tariffs through Section 301 and 232 investigations. This is an official position, not a final tariff adjustment. Because replacement tariffs applied, it is not a test of a one-sided repeal in October 2025. Sources: [19].

arguments.title: Removing barriers to poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Removing barriers to poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.

  • Because The reciprocal taxes threaten demand for these workers' goods. The October clothing study warns that “the elevated tariffs are set to reduce demand, squeeze suppliers, and depress investment in future capacity” [4].
  • Because This reaches an important source of women's earnings. UN Trade and Development's October 30 report states: “The textile and apparel industry, an important source of employment for women in many LDCs, has been hit hardest.” [20] LDCs are countries the U.N. classifies as least developed.
  • Because Workers can have few other ways to earn a living. The Fuller Project reports: “Women in Lesotho, Bangladesh and Cambodia all said there were no realistic employment alternatives available to them.” [21] A worker-rights researcher warns that if these jobs go, “workers will struggle to pay for basic necessities such as food, school fees, and healthcare” [21].
  • Because Lost sales and investment also threaten future opportunities. The U.N. report warns: “Higher levels of US protection on manufacturing, agriculture and food risk dampening LDCs’ hard-won progress in building productive capacities, reducing commodity dependence and promoting value addition.” [20] That means building the ability to make more goods, sell a wider range of products and do more of the work that adds to their value.
  • So Removing the added tax supports demand for workers' goods and investment in future production. That protects earnings for food, schooling and healthcare, women's ability to earn, and poorer countries' routes to better work. These are reasons for [NAME], who values protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.

arguments.title: Ending these taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 Ending these taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.

  • Because The emergency's stated problem is reflected in “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [10]. A trade deficit means the United States buys more goods from abroad than it sells abroad.
  • Because Small, poor economies have little ability to buy U.S. goods. The U.N. explains: “As many of these economies are small in size, structurally weak with low purchasing power, they offer limited export market opportunities for the US.” [22]
  • Because Lesotho shows the mismatch. Its share of the U.S. goods trade deficit in the U.N.'s 2024 data was tiny: “Lesotho 0.019%” [23]. It still faced an added tax under the later rates; September reporting describes “a much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21].
  • So Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people whose countries have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Fair treatment calls for burdens to reflect people's circumstances and their part in the problem. Sparing poor people this disproportionate burden serves [NAME]'s concern for justice across borders.
arguments.con_html:
Response The deficit-share comparison does not establish the unfair treatment it is used to prove.

  • Because The U.N.'s “Lesotho 0.019%” [23] measures a country’s share of the total U.S. goods trade deficit. The reported “much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21] measures a tax on the value of covered imports. Neither percentage measures the tax cost compared with a poor person’s income.
  • Because The PRO adds a rule that the burden is unjust because the country contributes little to the total deficit. [NAME]’s concern for just treatment of people does not by itself establish that national trade shares determine the burdens individuals should bear.
  • So A small country’s small share of a large country’s deficit is not a measure of injustice to its workers. The two percentages do not support the claimed disproportionate burden or show that ending it would correct unjust treatment.

paths.necessity_reason: The charge is removed only if the taxes stop on new imports from these countries.

arguments.title: Ending this use of emergency power checks burdens imposed without the usual required investigation.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Ending this use of emergency power checks burdens imposed without the usual required investigation.

  • Because The emergency powers law, called IEEPA, skips a check found in other main tariff laws. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, explains that it “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [24]
  • Because Careful review helps protect people who bear the costs. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce calls for “appropriate stakeholder consultation and a methodical assessment of costs” [8] before raising taxes on traded goods.
  • Because This bill makes Congress's power to end that use of emergency authority effective. CRS explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [24]
  • So People whose food budgets and jobs are at stake deserve public review of burdens placed on them. Ending this emergency enforces Congress's check on a route that does not require an investigation. That supports [NAME]'s concern that everyone be treated justly.

The Chamber letter says a more deliberative process could ensure consultation and lists S.J.Res.88 among responsive proposals. Sources: [10], [24], [8].

arguments.title: It removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.

  • Because The president of Unionwear, a U.S. maker, explains the price protection: “Each tariff increase reduces the cost advantage of imports, making our domestic production more competitive without us having to change anything.” [27] He also explains why taxes on the firm’s supplies do little to offset that benefit: “We source our raw materials domestically when possible, so tariffs on finished goods help us while tariffs on materials have minimal impact on our cost structure.” [27]
  • Because U.S. makers have reported winning work. Royal Apparel said: “Several production programs that were initially set to go overseas have now been redirected to Royal Apparel” [28].
  • Because This demand reaches employers that open doors to people with disabilities. The cofounder of Stakes Manufacturing said its April garment partnership would “meet the rising demand driven by recent tariff changes” [28]. Reporting on the firm found: “10% of the 225 employees at Stakes Manufacturing are people with an intellectual or developmental disability.” [29]
  • Because Earlier import shocks from China trade do not measure the effect of this change. They do show how hard lost factory work can be to replace for people without degrees: “Almost all of the manufacturing job losses affected workers without a college degree, and this group saw almost no job gains in the next two decades.” [30]
  • Because Those earlier import shocks also harmed children through their parents’ lost earnings. A study of trade shocks to young men’s relative earnings found that “these shocks heighten male idleness and premature mortality, and raise the share of mothers who are unwed and the share of children living in below-poverty, single-headed households.” [31]
  • So Removing this price protection puts vulnerable workers’ opportunities and their families’ security at risk. Protecting people who face barriers to work, and children who bear the costs of lost work, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Executive Order 14257 duties are added to other duties that the bill leaves in place. The redirected orders concern Royal Apparel and the disability-employment figure concerns Stakes; the Stakes statement refers to recent tariff changes generally. Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases had relative employment reductions, with a positive protection effect offset by input costs and retaliation. It names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. It reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result, and it does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [34].

arguments.title: Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.

  • Because Tariffs make goods from other countries cost more, which helps U.S. makers compete: “by making foreign goods more expensive, tariffs make domestic products more competitive.” [25] American Giant is one maker that produces in the United States: NPR reports that it “sources and manufactures almost all its products in the U.S., from cotton to the final stitch.” [26]
  • Because A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.” [27]
  • Because Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27]
  • Because Marriage and the husband's role as provider are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” [28] Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [28]
  • Because That family pattern also carries a duty to pass on the faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [28].
  • So By removing a defense against job and pay losses caused by imports, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
arguments.con_html:
Response A price advantage for U.S. products does not establish that these taxes protect the men's jobs and pay on which the family argument depends.

  • Because The bill says the April 2 emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] The comparison is keeping or ending its import taxes as of October 30, 2025.
  • Because The family study ties marriage losses to men's earnings compared with women's: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27] It studies rising Chinese import competition during 1990–2014, not the effects of these taxes.
  • Because A study of local employment under the 2018–2019 taxes reports that “import tariffs do not appear to increase employment in manufacturing” [29]. It directly tests the step from import protection to factory jobs, which the marriage study does not test.
  • Because A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–2019 taxes found that “a positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs.” [30]
  • Because For the 2025 taxes, the president of the textile trade group warned in October: “Reciprocal tariffs on these items hurt domestic textile producers and drives offshoring, undermining U.S. manufacturing jobs” [31]. She was discussing taxes on certain imported materials and machinery not available in the United States.
  • So American Giant's U.S. production and a price advantage do not establish that this extra tax layer preserves men's jobs or pay. Without that link, the historical import losses do not establish that ending these taxes puts marriage, husbands' provider roles or passing on the faith at greater risk.

original_mapping.title: It removes a country-based barrier to doing business with people despite disagreements with their governments.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes a country-based barrier to doing business with people despite disagreements with their governments.

  • Because The program applies across countries. It does not test each seller’s views: “all imports from all trading partners except as otherwise provided herein.” [3]
  • Because The April order makes agreement with U.S. policy one condition for lowering these taxes: “Should any trading partner take significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters, I may further modify the HTSUS to decrease or limit in scope the duties imposed under this order.” [3] The HTSUS is the official U.S. list of import tax rates.
  • Because The July revision again counted government alignment when setting rates, saying some partners “have failed to align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national-security matters.” [4]
  • So A willing seller and buyer face this added barrier because of where the goods come from, whatever the seller’s own views are. Ending it removes that penalty from their business ties, including ties across disagreements between governments.
  • Because Keeping willing relationships open without requiring agreement with people’s governments is one way to act on acceptance across national and political differences.
  • So [NAME]’s tolerance gives a reason to remove this barrier to accepting foreign people as business partners.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response The PRO leaves a gap between removing a cost on foreign goods and accepting foreign people across disagreements.

  • Because The taxes follow the product’s origin. Shipping guidance explains: “The tariffs are applied based upon the product’s country of origin rather than the country from which the product was shipped.” [5]
  • Because The condition for lowering rates concerns governments’ actions: “Should any trading partner take significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters, I may further modify the HTSUS to decrease or limit in scope the duties imposed under this order.” [3]
  • Because Where goods come from, what a government does, and whether people accept one another are different things. A product’s origin does not establish its seller’s nationality or views. A trade cost can apply within a relationship in which people already accept one another across differences.
  • So Removing this charge changes the terms of trade. The PRO still needs to explain why easing those terms puts acceptance of different people into practice. The government-alignment condition does not supply that link.
